title: The Solar System and Space Technologies
seo_title: Grade 9 Science: The Solar System and Space Technologies Worksheets (MATATAG)
standard_code: Grade 9, Quarter 2: Earth and Space Science
standard_text: The origin of the solar system; planets, comets and asteroids; galaxies and the universe; space technologies such as satellites and telescopes and their uses. (summary of the MATATAG Science curriculum, Grade 9, Quarter 2: Earth and Space Science)
meta_desc: Free Grade 9 Science worksheets (MATATAG, Quarter 2: Earth and Space Science): galaxies and the big bang, the origin of the solar system, the planets, satellites and telescopes and living and working in space. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago and is still expanding.
body_html:
How to think about it

The solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a spinning cloud of gas and dust (the nebular theory): the Sun formed at the center and planets formed from the disk around it. Comets and asteroids are leftover material. Distances in space are measured in astronomical units and light-years.

Evidence for the big bang includes the red shift of distant galaxies and the cosmic microwave background. Space technology such as satellites for weather, communication and GPS brings many benefits; the Philippines has launched its own microsatellites, such as Diwata-1 and Diwata-2, to observe the Earth.

Example

Light from a star takes 4 years to reach us. How far away is it?

Distance = 4 light-years

Answer: about 3.8 × 10¹³ km

Example

A galaxy's light is shifted towards red. What does this tell us?

The wavelength is stretched.

Answer: it is moving away from us

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a light-year is a unit of time.
  • Saying all stars end as black holes.
  • Thinking satellites stay up because there is no gravity in space.

faq.q: Why do we see distant galaxies as they were long ago?
faq.a: Their light took millions or billions of years to reach us.

faq.q: How do satellites help the Philippines?
faq.a: They track typhoons, map land and seas, and support communication and navigation.

sets.title: The origin of the solar system

items.q: In a star, 9 helium-4 nuclei combine step by step. What nucleus forms?
items.e: Mass number 4 × 9 = 36; atomic number 2 × 9 = 18 (argon).

items.q: Which evidence best supports this idea: “The Moon formed from material similar to Earth's, likely after a giant impact.”
c: Stromatolite fossils about 3.5 billion years old
Moon rocks brought back by Apollo
Heavily cratered surfaces on the Moon and Mercury
Banded iron formations about 2.5 billion years old
items.e: Match the evidence to the claim.

items.q: What does this evidence tell us about early Earth: Moon rocks brought back by Apollo?
c: The early solar system had many large impacts.
Earth had solid crust and probably liquid water very early.
The Moon formed from material similar to Earth's, likely after a giant impact.
The solar system, including Earth, formed about 4.56 billion years ago.
items.e: Old materials record early events.

items.q: In a star, 10 helium-4 nuclei combine step by step. What nucleus forms?
items.e: Mass number 4 × 10 = 40; atomic number 2 × 10 = 20 (calcium).

items.q: A rock has uranium-235 and lead-207 in a ratio of 1 : 31 (half-life of uranium-235: 704 million years). How old is it? (Assume all the lead-207 came from decay.)
items.e: 1 : 31 means 1/32 is left → 5 half-lives = 3,520 million years.

items.q: What does this evidence tell us about early Earth: Stromatolite fossils about 3.5 billion years old?
c: Oxygen began to build up in the oceans and air.
Simple microbial life existed very early.
The Moon formed from material similar to Earth's, likely after a giant impact.
The solar system, including Earth, formed about 4.56 billion years ago.
items.e: Old materials record early events.

items.q: In a massive star, 8 helium-4 nuclei (2 protons each) are built up into one nucleus. Which element is it?
items.e: 8 × 2 = 16 protons → sulfur.

items.q: Which happened first: oxygen begins to build up in the air, or the Moon forms after a giant impact?
c: the Moon forms after a giant impact
oxygen begins to build up in the air
They happened at the same time.
items.e: The Moon forms after a giant impact: about 4.5 billion years ago; oxygen begins to build up in the air: about 2.4 billion years ago.

items.q: In a star, 3 helium-4 nuclei combine step by step. What nucleus forms?
items.e: Mass number 4 × 3 = 12; atomic number 2 × 3 = 6 (carbon).

items.q: A rock has potassium-40 and argon-40 in a ratio of 1 : 7 (half-life of potassium-40: 1.25 billion years). How old is it? (Assume all the argon-40 came from decay.)
items.e: 1 : 7 means 1/8 is left → 3 half-lives = 3.75 billion years.

items.q: In a star, 5 helium-4 nuclei combine step by step. What nucleus forms?
items.e: Mass number 4 × 5 = 20; atomic number 2 × 5 = 10 (neon).

items.q: Which happened first: oxygen begins to build up in the air, or the oldest zircon crystals form?
c: They happened at the same time.
oxygen begins to build up in the air
items.e: The oldest zircon crystals form: about 4.4 billion years ago; oxygen begins to build up in the air: about 2.4 billion years ago.

items.q: In a massive star, 7 helium-4 nuclei (2 protons each) are built up into one nucleus. Which element is it?
items.e: 7 × 2 = 14 protons → silicon.

items.q: Which happened first: Earth forms, or the oldest zircon crystals form?
c: They happened at the same time.
items.e: Earth forms: about 4.56 billion years ago; the oldest zircon crystals form: about 4.4 billion years ago.

items.q: A mineral has 1/8 of its original uranium-235 left (half-life 704 million years). How old is it?
items.e: 1/8 = 3 half-lives; 3 × 704 = 2,112 million years.

items.q: Which happened first: Earth forms, or the first microbial fossils (stromatolites)?
c: They happened at the same time.
items.e: Earth forms: about 4.56 billion years ago; the first microbial fossils (stromatolites): about 3.5 billion years ago.

items.q: In a massive star, 3 helium-4 nuclei (2 protons each) are built up into one nucleus. Which element is it?
items.e: 3 × 2 = 6 protons → carbon.

items.q: Which happened first: the Late Heavy Bombardment of impacts, or the first animals appear?
c: They happened at the same time.
the Late Heavy Bombardment of impacts
items.e: The Late Heavy Bombardment of impacts: about 4 billion years ago; the first animals appear: about 0.6 billion years ago.

items.q: Which happened first: Earth forms, or the first animals appear?
c: They happened at the same time.
items.e: Earth forms: about 4.56 billion years ago; the first animals appear: about 0.6 billion years ago.

items.q: In a massive star, 9 helium-4 nuclei (2 protons each) are built up into one nucleus. Which element is it?
items.e: 9 × 2 = 18 protons → argon.

items.q: A person stands at a place on the right side of Earth. Which arrow shows the direction that Earth's gravity pulls on the person?
items.e: Gravity pulls toward the center of Earth, so arrow B (pointing into the globe) is “down” for this person.

items.q: Which object in the sky is a star?
items.e: The moon and planets reflect sunlight. The sun makes its own light.

items.q: Why are rockets launched with huge amounts of fuel?
c: Because space is full of air
They need a lot of thrust to escape Earth's gravity.
items.e: Leaving Earth takes a lot of energy.

items.q: A person stands at a place on the left side of Earth. Which arrow shows the direction that Earth's gravity pulls on the person?
items.e: Gravity pulls toward the center of Earth, so arrow C (pointing into the globe) is “down” for this person.

items.q: Why do astronauts exercise every day on the space station?
c: Without Earth's pull, their muscles and bones get weaker.
items.e: Exercise keeps them healthy.

items.q: A person stands at the North Pole. Which arrow shows the direction that Earth's gravity pulls on the person?
items.e: Gravity pulls toward the center of Earth, so arrow A (pointing into the globe) is “down” for this person.

items.q: What is a light-year?
c: the distance light travels in one year
the time it takes to see a star
items.e: A light-year is a distance: about 9.5 trillion kilometers.

items.q: Which is closest to Earth?
items.e: The sun is our closest star.

items.q: Why can't we see stars during the day?
c: Stars move away during the day.
The sun's bright light hides their dimmer light.
items.e: The stars are still there. Sunlight scattered in the sky outshines them.

items.q: A person stands at a place on the left side of Earth. Which arrow shows the direction that Earth's gravity pulls on the person?
items.e: Gravity pulls toward the center of Earth, so arrow D (pointing into the globe) is “down” for this person.

items.q: Which instrument lets you see craters on the Moon from your backyard?
items.e: Telescopes make faraway things look closer.

items.q: Why do astronauts float on the space station?
c: They and the station are falling around Earth together.
There is no gravity in space at all.
items.e: They are in constant free fall.

items.q: How did many Indigenous Peoples use the night sky?
c: to tell time, find directions and mark seasons
items.e: Star knowledge is passed down through stories.

items.q: A star looks very dim from Earth. Which could be true?
c: It must be smaller than a house.
It may be very far away.
It must not give off light.
items.e: Distance can make even a very bright star look dim.

items.q: Why does the sun look much brighter than other stars?
c: Other stars are turned off in the day.
It is much closer to Earth than any other star.
It is the only star that gives off light.
items.e: The sun is about 150 million km away. The next closest star is about 270,000 times farther.

items.q: Why do astronauts wear space suits on a spacewalk?
c: to give air and protect them from extreme temperatures and radiation
items.e: Space has no air to breathe.

items.q: A person stands at the North Pole. Which arrow shows the direction that Earth's gravity pulls on the person?
items.e: Gravity pulls toward the center of Earth, so arrow C (pointing into the globe) is “down” for this person.

items.q: Which statement about stars is true?
c: All stars are smaller than Earth.
Many stars are as big as or bigger than the sun.
Stars are closer than the moon.
Stars are holes in the sky.
items.e: Stars look like tiny dots only because they are so far away.

items.q: What is space junk?
c: old satellites and pieces of rockets orbiting Earth
items.e: It can hit working satellites.

items.q: What is the Sun?
items.e: Our nearest star.

items.q: Which kind of orbit keeps a satellite above the same spot on the equator?
items.e: At about 36 000 km up, the satellite circles once a day, matching Earth's rotation.

items.q: What keeps the Moon in orbit around the Earth?
c: the gravitational pull of the Earth
items.e: Mass (kg) stays the same; weight (N) depends on gravity.

items.q: Why do astronauts on the space station exercise every day?
c: in microgravity, bones and muscles weaken because they do not support the body's weight
to make electricity for the station
items.e: Treadmills, bikes and resistance machines slow bone and muscle loss.

items.q: Does Earth's gravity reach the Moon?
c: No, it stops at the atmosphere.
Yes. It keeps the Moon in orbit.
items.e: Gravity reaches far into space.

items.q: How can satellite data help farmers?
c: images show which parts of a field are dry, unhealthy or need fertilizer
satellites stop insects from eating crops
satellites make the growing season longer
items.e: This is called precision agriculture.

items.q: Which is a risk to astronauts' health on long missions?
c: bone and muscle loss in microgravity and higher radiation
items.e: Astronauts exercise about two hours a day on the space station.

items.q: Why are many telescopes placed in space instead of on the ground?
c: there is more light in space at night
stars are much closer in orbit
telescopes are cheaper to build in space
Earth's atmosphere blurs light and absorbs some wavelengths, such as X-rays and much infrared
items.e: The James Webb Space Telescope observes infrared light that the atmosphere would block.

items.q: Why do astronauts need spacesuits on a spacewalk?
c: the suits stop gravity from acting
space has no air to breathe, almost no pressure, extreme temperatures and strong radiation
the suits let them breathe the gases in space
items.e: The suit is a small spacecraft with its own air, pressure, cooling and radiation shield.

items.q: Which planet takes the shortest time to orbit the Sun?
items.e: It is closest: about 88 days.

items.q: What powers most satellites and the space station?
items.e: Sunlight is strong and constant in orbit, and the panels charge batteries for the dark part of each orbit.

items.q: Which instrument on a satellite measures heat given off by the ground and oceans?
items.e: Warm objects give off infrared radiation, so the sensor can map temperatures.

items.q: What do rovers on Mars do?
c: drive on the surface and study rocks, soil and air
items.e: Rovers are robots controlled from Earth.

items.q: What is space debris?
c: clouds of gas around the Sun
old satellites, rocket stages and fragments left in orbit
items.e: Even small pieces move at about 28 000 km/h and can damage working spacecraft.

items.q: Why do outer planets take longer to orbit the Sun?
c: They travel a longer path and move more slowly because the Sun's pull is weaker.
items.e: Distance matters.

items.q: What shape are most planetary orbits?
items.e: Slightly stretched circles.

items.q: Why do some Indigenous knowledge keepers and scientists both study the night sky?
c: stars can be seen only from space
the sky has been used for navigation, calendars and stories for thousands of years
the sky only changes once a century
items.e: Many peoples used star patterns to mark seasons for hunting, fishing and planting.

items.q: What is the gravitational field strength on the Earth?
items.e: More precisely 9.8 N/kg.

items.q: What is 1 astronomical unit (AU)?
c: the average distance from Earth to the Sun, about 150 million km
items.e: Used for solar system distances.

items.q: What two things make an orbit?
c: forward motion and gravity pulling toward the center
items.e: Gravity curves the path.
